explanation:
Confabulation may be spontaneous where often elements of fantasy are found. It can also occur in an attempt to avoid embarrassment as in this case. Confabulation is the process of describing plausibly false memories for a period for which the patient has amnesia. Two broad patterns emerge: the embarrassed type, in which the patient tries to fill in gaps in memory as a result of awareness of a deficit, and the fantastic type, in which the lacunae are in filled in by details exceeding the need of the memory impairment such as descriptions of wild adventures. Perseveration is characterised by continuing with a verbal response or action that was initially appropriate after it ceases to be apposite. It is associated with organic brain disease and is occasionally seen in schizophrenia.

This patient is highly suggestible as she answers yes to closed questions and admits to the emotions in any random picture shown to her. Suggestibility is a propensity to be abnormally compliant with suggestions, commands, directions, instructions, or orders from another person.

Neuroanatomical lesions in CNS disorders For each of the condition below choose the most specific option/s from given list Occipitotemporal junction Corpus callosum Inferior frontal gyrus Korsakoff psychosis Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex Third ventricle Gerstmann syndrome Dorsomedial thalamus Supramarginal gyrus Hippocampus Prosopagnosia Hypothalamus

Alzheimer disease
correctAnswer: Korsakoff psychosis → Dorsomedial thalamus, Gerstmann syndrome → Supramarginal gyrus, Prosopagnosia → Occipitotemporal junction, Alzheimer disease → Hippocampus
explanation:
About 80 per cent of alcoholic patients recovering from Wernicke encephalopathy develop Korsakoff amnesic syndrome. Diagnosis of Korsakoff syndrome correlates best with the presence of lesions in the dorsomedial thalamus. But lesions in the mammillary bodies, the mammillothalamic tract and the anterior thalamus may be more relevant to memory dysfunction than lesions in the medial dorsal nucleus of the thalamus (Kopelamn et al., 2009). Gerstmann syndrome is characterized by four primary symptoms: Dysgraphia/agraphia, Dyscalculia/acalculia, Finger agnosia and Left-right disorientation. This is often associated with brain lesions in the dominant (usually left) side of the angular and supramarginal gyri (parietal lobe). Prosopagnosics cannot recognise familiar faces. Face processing is a bilateral function; more vital areas may be present on the right hemisphere. Acquired prosopagnosia is usually associated with bilateral or right-sided lesions of the occipital - temporal junction (fusiform gyrus).

In Alzheimer disease, the main areas affected are the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe. Atrophic changes are mainly observed in these two areas in even in very early stages of Alzheimer disease. Barton, JJ., (2008). Prosopagnosia associated with a left occipitotemporal lesion. Excerpt retrieved from http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18374372 Kopeman et al., (2009). stem: Which of the following antipsychotics is the fastest to dissociate from the dopamine D2 receptor?
explanation: Clozapine is an antagonist of 5-HT2A, D1, D3, and D4. It also has potent antagonism of muscarinic M1, H1, and alpha-1 adrenergic receptors. It has relatively low potency as a D2 receptor antagonist. At therapeutic doses, clozapine occupies fewer D2 receptors than the other drugs that treat psychosis. Clinically effective doses of clozapine occupy only 40-50% of striatal D2 receptors. This is probably why clozapine has low propensity to cause EPS. It has also been postulated that clozapine binds more loosely to the D2 receptor, and because of this ‘fast dissociation’, more normal dopamine neurotransmission is possible.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 613. Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5 th Edition. 2021. p. 225.

stem: Gamma hydroxybutyrate (GHB) acts on which of the following receptors?
explanation: Sodium oxybate is also known as gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), and acts as a full agonist at GHB receptors and a partial agonist at GABA-B receptors. GHB is a natural product in the brain and formed by the neurotransmitter GABA. It has been labeled a ‘date rape’ drug as it can be used with alcohol for this purpose, knocking someone out and causing amnesia for the time while involuntarily intoxicated. Because it profoundly increases slow-wave sleep and the growth hormone surge that accompanies slow wave sleep, it was also used (abused) by athletes as a performance-enhancing drug, especially in the 1980s when it was sold over the counter in health food stores. GHB is used in some European countries as a treatment for alcoholism.

stem: A 60-year-old gentleman has a diagnosis of bipolar affective disorder and is on Lithium carbonate. He has recently developed systemic hypertension. Which one among the following is the most appropriate drug to treat his hypertension?
explanation: ACE inhibitors (e.g. captopril) can reduce thirst (which can lead to mild dehydration) and increase renal sodium loss (leading to increased sodium re-absorption by the kidney), resulting in an increase in lithium plasma levels. The magnitude of this effect is variable, from no increase to a four-fold increase. Diuretics can reduce the renal clearance of lithium, the magnitude of this effect being greater with thiazide than loop diuretics. Lithium levels usually rise within 10 days of a thiazide diuretic (e.g. bendroflumethiazide, chlortalidone, inadapamide, xipamide) being prescribed. Although there are case reports of lithium toxicity induced by loop diuretics, many patients receive loop diuretics (e.g. furosemide) together with lithium without apparent problems.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 252-253.

explanation: The most worrisome side effect of MAOIs is the tyramine-induced hypertensive crisis (‘cheese reaction’). The amino acid tyramine is normally transformed via GI metabolism. However, MAOIs inactivate GI metabolism of dietary tyramine, thus allowing intact tyramine to enter the circulation. A hypertensive crisis may subsequently occur because of a powerful pressor effect of the amino acid. Sources of dietary tyramine include cheese, meat extracts and yeast extracts, alcohol, non-fresh fish, non-fresh poultry, offal, avocado, banana skins, broad bean pods, caviar, and herring (pickled or smoked). Unlike the others listed, grapefruit juice is not rich in tyramine.

Ependymal cells are a particular type of glia that cover the ventricles and enable CSF circulation. Specialised ependymal cells form the choroid plexus.

correctAnswer: An 18-year-old man is in the process of developing a sense of identity when he leaves home to join the military. Here he has the opportunity to learn and develop new skills, which later on in life are incorporated into his sense of self. → Identity Moratorium, A 17-year-old woman spends most of her time outdoors, in the company of a mixed group of young people. They spend time drinking alcohol, smoking cannabis; they have no plans for the future. → Identity Diffusion, A 17-year-old man is given the choice by his parents to stop attending church if he wishes to. He doesn't wish to make an exploration of his own, but continues to attend church with his family, and to conform to their way of practicing religion. → Identity Foreclosure, A 21-year-old man after a lengthy period of exploration and self- searching, feels that he has a steady and stable sense of self. He finds himself committed to his work, with a clear sense of his goals and beliefs. → Identity Achievement
explanation:
Marcia distinguished four identity statuses based on the amount of exploration and commitment the adolescent experiences or has experienced

1) Identity Moratorium: This is a stage in which identity achievement is postponed whilst an intense exploration, which may be experienced as a crisis. At this point the young person is not yet ready to make a firm commitment.

2) Identity Diffusion: Identity issues have not been considered in detail and no firm commitments have been made for the future. During this stage the individual does not commit to any goals; it is characterized by procrastination, avoidance of responsibility and is the opposite of identity achievement.

3) Identity Foreclosure: Identity issues have not been considered seriously but future commitments have been made in spite of this. In this stage teenagers accept and adopt the traditional values and cultural norms of their parents or surrounding culture, rather than exploring and forming their own.

4) Identity Achievement: Various alternatives have been carefully considered and firm future commitments have been made. In this stage the individual is said to have solved their identity crisis and is able to make commitments to goals, values and beliefs.

stem: Repeated grandiose lies of a patient who seems to believe in his own untruthful statements is best described as
explanation: Pseudologia fantastica is typified by these characteristics: (1) the stories are not entirely improbable and are often built upon a matrix of truth; (2) the stories are enduring; (3) the stories are not told for personal profit per se and have a self-aggrandizing quality; and (4) they are distinct from delusions in that the person, when confronted with facts, can acknowledge these falsehoods. Pseudologica fantastica is referred to by various names: ‘pathological lying’, ‘mythomania’, and ‘deception syndrome’, among others. It is significantly different than mere lying. It involves disproportionate falsifications that may be extensive and complicated, present over a period of years or a lifetime, with no external gain or motive. In other words, this lying serves no obvious purpose, appears impulsive, and may be associated with an element of ‘dyscontrol’. It is often associated with antisocial personality disorder, narcissistic personality disorder, borderline personality disorder, histrionic personality disorder, and PTSD. However, it is most often associated with factitious disorder, which is conceptualised as the intentional production of physical or psychological signs or symptoms for no obvious external gain and without clear reasoning behind the behaviour.

Projection is characterised as perceiving and reacting to unacceptable inner impulses and their derivations as though they were outside the self. On a psychotic level, this takes the form of frank delusions about external reality, usually persecutory, and includes both perceptions of one’s own feelings and those of another with subsequent acting on the perception (psychotic paranoid delusions).

Projection is a primitive or immature defense mechanism that involves attributing one’s own internal unacceptable ideas and impulses to an external target, such as another individual, and reacting accordingly to them. stem: Tarasoff case is related to which of the following ethical principles?
explanation: On 27 October 1969, Tatiana Tarasoff was killed by her ex-boyfriend (Mr. P), who had previously declared his intentions during an appointment with his psychotherapist at the University of California at Berkley. The therapist notified the campus police, both orally and in writing, that the patient was dangerous and should be committed. Concerned about the breach of confidentiality, the therapist’s supervisor vetoed the recommendation and ordered all records related to the patient’s treatment destroyed. At the same time, the campus police temporarily detained Mr. P, but then released him. Two months later, Mr. P killed Tatiana. Her parents sued the university, and the Supreme Court ultimately decided that physicians and therapists have a duty to warn third parties of threatened danger arising from a patient’s violent intentions. As a final statement, the Court stated that ‘protective privilege ends where public peril begins.’
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 970. Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 839.

stem: According to the Holmes and Rahe Social readjustment scale, which of the following has the highest 'Life Change' value?
explanation: In 1967, psychiatrists Thomas Holmes and Richard Rahe examined over 5000 patients’ medical records to determine whether stressful events cause illnesses. Patients ranked a list of 43 life events based on a relative score. Each event had a different ‘weight’ for stress. Their results were published as the Social Readjustment Rating Scale, now commonly known as the Holmes and Rahe Stress Scale. The scale lists common stressful events and arbitrarily assigns a value of 50 Life Change Units (LCUs) to the stress caused by marriage. Death of a spouse has the highest LCUs at 100, followed by divorce (73 LCUs), and marital separation (65 LCUs).
reference: Noone PA. The Holmes–Rahe Stress Inventory. Occupational Medicine. 2017 Oct 1;67(7):581-2. Holmes TH, Rahe RH. The social readjustment rating scale. Journal of psychosomatic research. 1967.

stem: Which of the following ethical theories concerns itself with the intent behind the actions of an individual, rather than the consequences?
explanation: According to Immanuel Kant, a German philosopher, deontology is an ethical approach centered on rules and professional duties. Unlike many ethical theories, deontology does not focus on the consequences of individual actions. Personal emotions behind actions also do not matter with Kantian deontology because Kant believed humans do not always have rational control over their feelings. Instead, the intent behind chosen actions holds far more importance. Therefore, deontology proponents judge actions based on what people consider to be morally correct, regardless of actual consequences.

stem: Which of the following experiments is not correctly matched with Piaget's stages of cognitive development?
options: Classification of objects according to rules - concrete operational stage
explanation: In the sensorimotor stage (birth to 2 years), infants learn to differentiate themselves from the world. They also become able to maintain a mental image of an object, even when it is not visible (object permanence). The lack of mastery of conservation in children at the pre-operational stage was demonstrated by Jean Piaget through a series of experiments. He also used the ‘three mountains task’ to demonstrate that pre-operational children comprehend the world only from their own point of view and demonstrate ‘egocentrism’. It is not until the stage of concrete operations that egocentric thought is replaced by operational thought. Children can now see things from someone else’s perspective. Children also understand the concept of conservation, which is the ability to recognise that, although the shape of objects may change, the objects still maintain or conserve other characteristics that enable them to be recognised as the same. Piaget and Inhelder demonstrated that children's understanding of the physical world changes with growth by using pendulum experiment. At the start of formal operational thinking, children can construct experiments to deduct facts. They can work out the factor that determines swinging duration as string length and not weight or speed, etc.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 1007-1009. Colman AM. Oxford Dictionary of Psychology, 4 th Edition. 2015. p. 237.

stem: Which of the following is NOT an effect of parental divorce?
options: Guilt and accepting responsibility for separation
explanation: A child’s age at the time of the divorce affects the child’s reaction to the divorce. Immediately after a divorce, an increase in behavioural and emotional disorders appears in all age groups. Infants do not understand anything about separation or divorce. However, they do notice changes in their parents’ responses to them and may experience changes in their eating or sleeping patterns; have bowel problems; and seem more fretful, fearful, or anxious. Children 3-6 years of age may not understand what is happening, and those who do understand often assume that they are somehow responsible for the divorce. Older children, especially adolescents, comprehend the situation and may believe that they could have prevented the divorce had they intervened in some way, but they are still hurt, angry, and critical. Among boys, physical aggression is a common sign of distress. Suicide rates for children of divorce are much higher than for children from intact families.

stem: Benzodiazepine withdrawal is associated with:
explanation: Benzodiazepines belong to a class of drugs that modulate the neurotransmitter GABA, particularly GABA A to open the chloride channel. They can modulate GABA A receptors as an agonist. People become tolerant to benzodiazepines probably because their nerve cells respond by producing fewer receptors for GABA/benzodiazepines. This phenomenon, known as 'down-regulation', means that the number of 'high affinity' GABA receptors decreases in response to the enhancement of GABA caused by the drug. The body responds to the continued presence of the drug with a series of adjustments that tend to overcome the drug effects. In the case of benzodiazepines, compensatory changes occur in the GABA and benzodiazepine receptors which become less responsive, so that the inhibitory actions of GABA and benzodiazepines are decreased (Ref: CH Ashton. The role of GABA and GABA receptors in benzodiazepine withdrawal. http://www.benzosupport.org/gaba.htm)

stem: Which one among the following is a neuropsychological theory of ADHD?
explanation: Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder has been implicated in dysfunction of neural reward circuitry controlling motivation, reward, and impulsivity, including orbitofrontal cortex systems. This condition has increasingly been defined as a disorder resulting from impaired behavioral inhibition leading to executive function deficits. ADHD patients have deficits in higher-level cognitive functions necessary for mature adult goal-directed behaviours, in so-called ‘executive functions’ (EFs), that are mediated by late developing fronto-striato-parietal and fronto-cerebellar networks. The most consistent findings are in so-called ‘cool’ EF such as motor response inhibition, working memory, sustained attention, response variability, and cognitive switching as well as in temporal processing, with most consistent deficits in time discrimination and estimation tasks.

explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is routinely used in the acute care setting after traumatic brain injury (TBI) to guide decisions in triage, based on its ability to predict mortality. Although the GCS has been previously demonstrated to predict mortality, efficacy in the prediction of functional outcome is not well established. GCS less than 8 can mean a mortality rate as high as 70%. In the lower ranges of GCS score, there is a direct linear relation to a poor outcome including severe neurological disability, vegetative state and death. stem: The term used for the purpose of identifying the locus of a gene on the chromosome by studying the extent to which it co-segregates with a marker gene is called
explanation: Linkage analysis is used to obtain a coarse chromosomal location of the genes associated with a phenotype under investigation (e.g. a genetic disease or an important quantitative trait). All genetic mapping methods aim to identify disease-associated variants based on their chromosomal position and the principle of genetic linkage. Genes that are physically close to one another on a chromosome are genetically linked, and those that are further apart or are on different chromosomes are genetically unlinked. Unlinked genes will recombine at random. Genetic loci that are linked will recombine less frequently than expected by random segregation, with the degree of recombination proportional to the physical distance between them.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 988.

stem: The term used to describe a point mutation that leads to failure of expression of alleles is
explanation: Loss-of-function mutations are the result of gene product having less or no function. Phenotypes associated with such mutations are most often recessive. Loss-of-function mutations abolish a gene’s biomolecular activity. The existence of a category of alleles distinguished by a derived loss of biochemical functions has been described by various names: amorphic, loss-of-function, non-functional, knockout, null, pseudogene, or gene loss. Total gene loss is the most obvious case of loss of function. Yet total gene loss is not the only means by which loss of function can occur. Single mutations and many mutation types such as premature stop codons, frameshifts, splice site disruptions, and elimination of regulatory regions required for gene expression can have effects that are functionally indistinguishable from complete gene loss.
reference: Monroe JG, McKay JK, Weigel D, Flood PJ. The population genomics of adaptive loss of function. Heredity. 2021 Mar;126(3):383-95.

stem: Which of the following disorders is associated with HLA-DQB1*-0602?
explanation: Narcolepsy is a chronic disorder that is primarily characterised by excessive daytime sleepiness and, in most individuals, cataplexy. The latest edition of the International Classification of Sleep Disorders has reclassified narcolepsy into narcolepsy type 1 (NT1) and NT2. This is based on the finding that the absence of the hypocretin peptides (also known as orexins; which are neuropeptides with a role in the regulation of sleep and wakefulness) is a fundamental marker in most patients with narcolepsy with cataplexy. Patients with NT1 have cataplexy and/or low levels of hypocretin 1 (also known as orexin A) in the CSF, whereas patients with NT2 do not have cataplexy and have normal levels of hypocretin 1. The main genetic risk for narcolepsy is the HLA-DQB1*06:02 allele, which explains the majority of the known genetic effects in NT1. Depending on the population, 86-98% of patients with NT1 carry the HLA-DQB1*06:02 allele.
reference: Kornum BR et al. Narcolepsy. Nature reviews Disease primers. 2017 Feb 9;3(1):1-9.
